profile.campus: Sandston, Henrico County, Virginia (QTS Richmond 1 campus)
profile.reading:
RIC1 DC2 is one of six operating buildings, DC1 through DC6, that make up QTS's Richmond 1 (RIC1) data center campus in Sandston, an unincorporated community in eastern Henrico County just outside Richmond. Per QTS's own site, the RIC1 campus spans 207 acres, totals 2.3 million square feet of built space, and provides 238 megawatts of campus power capacity, a figure QTS states at the campus level across all six buildings rather than broken out per building. DC1, DC2, and DC3 share the mailing address 6000 Technology Blvd, Sandston, VA 23150, while DC4, DC5, and DC6, mapped separately in this registry, carry their own addresses on nearby Portugee Road, all within the same RIC1 campus tract. No operator source found in this research disaggregates DC2's own IT load, utility service size, standby generation, or onsite generation from that campus total, so none of the four power figures this registry tracks are asserted for this specific building.

QTS (the operator name on this row, Quality Technology Services, is the company's pre 2013 name, it now operates as QTS Realty Trust under the domain q.com) was founded in 2003 in Overland Park, Kansas, went public in 2013, and per Blackstone's own press release was taken private in a roughly 10 billion dollar acquisition by Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust and affiliated funds completed August 31, 2021, at 78 dollars a share. The company lists its US headquarters at 22271 Broderick Drive, Sterling, Virginia, in the Northern Virginia data center corridor, and separately maintains an operations support presence in Suwanee, Georgia.

The RIC1 campus sits inside the much larger White Oak Technology Park, which Henrico County's own 2024 planning staff analysis describes as hosting 37 data centers of varying sizes from multiple operators, QTS and Meta among them, on land associated with a former semiconductor manufacturing site. Henrico's Board of Supervisors approved a related rezoning to light industrial for an adjacent roughly 622 acre QTS expansion tract on May 14, 2024, following an April 2024 Planning Commission recommendation, and on May 16, 2024 the Board separately established a 60 million dollar affordable housing trust fund financed by data center real estate tax revenue, according to Virginia Business. That expansion tract, assembled through a December 2023 purchase from Harmon family interests and a June 2024 purchase of additional acreage from developer Hourigan for roughly 118.8 million dollars, is reported by Richmond BizSense to be planned for up to 17 additional buildings across roughly 1,100 acres under the RIC4 and RIC5 project names, separate QTS phases from RIC1 and not part of this campus. The Virginia State Corporation Commission approved a related Dominion Energy application in March 2024 for two new 230 kilovolt transmission lines to serve the area's growing data center load. Henrico's staff analysis also proposes a new Technology Boulevard special focus overlay of roughly 3,100 acres and nearly 80 parcels covering White Oak and adjoining land, a sign the county is actively working to manage further growth rather than treating existing campuses like RIC1 as a closed matter. No county building permit, assessor parcel record, or Uptime Institute tier certificate specific to DC2 was located in this research session, and building level detail for DC2 remains genuinely unpublished rather than merely unresearched.

reading.body:
RIC1 DC2 is one of six buildings on the Richmond 1 campus in Sandston, Virginia, a former semiconductor plant that QTS has operated since 2010. QTS publishes only a campus-wide aggregate of 238 megawatts across all six buildings and 2.3 million square feet, without breaking down power or space per building. No building-level specifications for DC2 itself are published, so the contribution of this specific facility to state or national AI compute capacity cannot be stated from available data.

The RIC1 campus sits within a much larger White Oak Technology Park that Henrico County's planning staff counts as hosting 37 data centers from multiple operators. Virginia has approved two new 230-kilovolt transmission lines to serve the region's data center load growth as of March 2024, and has mapped 330 data center facilities statewide, of which only 25 publish power figures totaling 1,603 megawatts. The RIC1 campus ranks 26th among those 25 published megawatt figures in Virginia, though that ranking applies to the entire six-building campus, not to DC2 alone.

The LEED Gold certification qualifies the RIC1 campus for efficient facilities operations. County planning documents from 2024 show Henrico is actively managing data center growth through zoning overlays and expansion reviews rather than treating RIC1 as settled infrastructure, signaling continued regulatory attention to the region's cumulative data center footprint and grid demands.
